title: Science: Weather and Water on the Move
theme: Weather, climate, and the water cycle
objectives: I can use science words to explain how water moves from the ground to the sky and back.
I can tell the difference between weather and climate.
I can use exact words for rain, wind, heat, and cold.
I can write a weather report using words from this unit.
rationale: This cross-curricular science unit anchors three Tier 3 water-cycle terms (evaporate, precipitation, climate) with Tier 2 describing words students need to read and write about weather in any subject. The ten words sort into the science of weather (evaporate, precipitation, climate, forecast), rain, wind, and dry spells (drizzle, gust, drought), and temperature and air (humid, frigid, scorching). Students build precise ladders for rain and temperature, learn that weather is what happens today and climate is the pattern over years, and reuse moist, dense, and towering from earlier units.

passage.title: Water on the Move
paras: Water is always on the move. When the sun warms a lake or an ocean, some of the water will evaporate and rise into the air as a gas. High up, the air is cold, so the gas cools and forms tiny drops that make clouds.

When the drops in a cloud grow heavy, they fall as precipitation. It may be a light drizzle or a pounding storm. If the air is very cold, it falls as snow or hail instead. The water then flows into streams and soaks into moist soil, and the cycle begins again.

Weather changes from day to day. A forecast tells us what to expect, such as a gust of wind, a humid afternoon, or a frigid night. Climate is different. It is the usual weather in a place over many years. In a desert, summer days can be scorching, while Antarctica stays frigid all year.

Sometimes a place gets too little precipitation for a long time. That is called a drought. Plants dry up and rivers shrink. Scientists study clouds and temperatures to make better forecasts so that people can prepare.

choices: Clouds form when the air cools.

qs.why: Dying plants and shrinking rivers show the harm done by too little rain.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: How water moves and how we describe weather and climate
How to build a rain gauge
qs.why: The paragraphs explain the water cycle and the difference between weather and climate.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten weather and water words, use them to describe the water cycle and weather reports, and separate weather from climate. They build ladders for rain and temperature and write a short weather report.

notes.va.evaporate.v: Evaporate is a Tier 3 science word. Students often say the water disappears. Correct it: it changes into water vapor, a gas in the air. Draw an arrow from the puddle up to the sky.
notes.va.precipitation.n: Precipitation is the umbrella word. Have students list the kinds and sort pictures into rain, snow, sleet, and hail.
notes.va.climate.n: Weather is today; climate is the pattern. Use the clothes test: weather is what you wear today, climate is what is in your closet.
notes.va.forecast.n: Forecast is a prediction. Ask why a forecast can be wrong. Forecast is also a verb; show the example in the senses field but keep practice on the noun.
notes.va.drizzle.n: Drizzle sits at the gentle end of the rain ladder. Build the ladder: drizzle, shower, downpour.
notes.va.humid.adj: Humid is about water in the air, not the ground. Compare it with moist from unit 2: moist is a little wet to the touch; humid is wet air.
notes.va.gust.n: A gust is brief. Ask students to contrast a gust with a steady breeze using their hands: short push, long flow.
notes.va.drought.n: A drought is long, not one dry day. Link to climate: a drought is a long departure from the usual rainfall pattern.
notes.va.frigid.adj: Frigid is at the cold end of the temperature ladder. Students may confuse frigid and rigid because of the sound; draw the letter f.
notes.va.scorching.adj: Scorching is at the hot end of the temperature ladder. Build a ladder with frigid, cool, warm, hot, scorching.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says the water will evaporate and rise into the air as a gas. I know the puddle does not disappear; it changes into a gas I cannot see. I can draw an arrow from the puddle up to the sky and write evaporate beside it.'
